functions.name: Signing in
functions.summary: Lets a person sign in to Vennusign — either by going through Google, Apple, or the Vennusign login page, or by asking for a one-time link emailed to them and clicking it. It also signs them back out again.

lives.who: Anyone signing in — venue owners and staff using the customer login

functions.name: Proving it is really you
functions.summary: Lets an account holder prove they really are who they say they are, using either a passkey (fingerprint, face, or device PIN) or a six-digit code from an authenticator app, with one-time backup codes if they lose the phone. It also covers signing in with a passkey in the first place, and adding, renaming or removing the passkeys on the account.

functions.name: Who am I and what can I do
functions.summary: This is the check the app makes the moment someone opens it: it says who is signed in, which venue they are working in, which other venues they can switch to, and which parts of the product are switched on for them. Every screen in the back office and the support console relies on this answer to decide what to show.

lives.who: Venue owners signing in with their own account

functions.builtTwice: Yes — this is built three separate times, for three separate audiences, one endpoint each. The venue staff version (BackOfficeSessionController) answers who you are, which venue you are in, which venues you may switch to, and which features are on. The venue owner sign-in version (CustomerAuthenticationController) answers only who the person is — id, email, display name, and how they signed in. The platform staff version (PlatformOperationsSessionController) answers who is signed in and which areas of the support console to show. All three are live and in use, and a change to what a session tells the app has to be made in each one that needs it.

functions.name: Setting up a new venue
functions.summary: This is how a brand-new customer gets set up: they create their business record, then create their venue with its name, timezone, venue type and languages, and can check at any point how far through that setup they have got. There is also a bare venue-create endpoint that makes a venue record on its own, outside the guided signup steps.

lives.who: Anyone calling it — this one asks for no sign-in at all

functions.builtTwice: Yes — this function is built in two separate places. One is the guided signup path at /api/customer-onboarding (3 endpoints: check setup progress, create the business, create the venue), used by new customers signing themselves up and requiring a signed-in customer with second-factor sign-in satisfied. The other is a standalone venue-create endpoint at /api/venues (1 endpoint), which creates the same venue record — name, timezone, type, languages — but takes no sign-in at all. Both are live code and both have to keep working, so a change to how a venue is created (a new field, a new rule, a new default) has to be made in both places or the two will drift apart.

functions.name: Plans and paying
functions.summary: This is how a venue picks a plan and pays for it. A new customer signing up can see the plans on offer, start a free trial, or go straight to a card payment page; an existing venue owner can see what plan they are on, how much of their screen and venue allowance they are using, what other plans they could move to and what they would lose by moving, and can open Stripe to change plan or update their card.
functions.builtTwice: Yes — paying for a plan is built twice, in two separate places serving two different audiences. The signup build (CustomerOnboardingController, 3 endpoints) serves someone who is not a paying customer yet: it lists the plans on offer, starts a free trial, and hands them a Stripe payment page. The billing build (BackOfficeBillingController, 4 endpoints) serves a venue owner already signed in: it shows their current plan and their usage against their limits, and opens Stripe to buy a plan, switch plan, or update payment details. Both are live and both are called, so a change to how plans or payment work — a new plan, a change to what a plan includes, a change to how eligibility is checked before someone can buy — has to be made in both places, not one.

functions.name: Renting screen hardware
functions.summary: A venue owner can rent their screen hardware from Vennusign instead of buying it, paying for a fixed-term bundle of screens through the normal card checkout. This is the one step that starts that rental purchase.

functions.name: Revenue and the platform dashboard
functions.summary: Lets Vennusign's own staff see what the business is earning: how much subscription money is coming in each month and each year, split by plan, plus a month-by-month history of the last two years. It also points out any price set up in the payment system that isn't tied to a plan, so nothing is being charged without a home.

functions.name: Menus
functions.summary: This is the shelf of menus a venue keeps: staff can see every menu they have, create a new empty one, rename it, copy one, and put an old one away (or bring it back). It also tells the menu builder the basics it needs to work — the venue's timezone, its size limits, and how many menus it is allowed versus how many it has already used.
functions.builtTwice: Yes — this function is built twice, in two separate places. The venue-staff build is the full one: 10 endpoints spread across two controllers (BackOfficeContentController with 7, BackOfficeMenusController with 3), and it is what venue managers use to list, create, rename, copy and archive their menus. The platform-staff build is separate and much smaller: 1 read-only endpoint in PlatformOperationsMenusController that lets a Vennusign support person look at a venue's menus, sections and items without changing anything. Both are live and both are called, so any change to how menus are listed or read has to be made in every place it is built.

functions.name: Pages and sections
functions.summary: Lets venue staff lay out a menu: create, rename, reorder, copy and remove the pages of a menu, and add, rename, reorder, move and remove the sections (like "Starters" or "Desserts") that sit on those pages. Deleting a page or section asks what should happen to what was on it — move it elsewhere or send it back to the library — and reordering refuses if someone else changed things first.

functions.name: Dishes and the item library
functions.summary: Lets venue staff build up the actual dishes on a menu — add a dish to a section (picking one from the venue's saved dish library or typing a brand new one), edit its name, description or price, drag it between sections, reorder it, and take it off a page without losing it from the library. The dish library itself is searchable, and it tells you which menus a dish is already on.

functions.name: Marking things sold out
functions.summary: Lets venue staff flag a dish as sold out — or put it back on sale — and the change shows on every screen straight away, with no need to republish the menu. Staff can also see what is currently marked sold out, who did it and when, and put everything back on sale in one go.
functions.builtTwice: Yes — this is built twice, both times for venue staff, in two different controllers. The main build (BackOfficeContentController, 4 endpoints) powers the dedicated sold-out screen: the one-page view of what is live and what is off, marking an item sold out or back on, the list of what is currently off with who changed it and when, and putting everything back on at once. The second build (BackOfficeMenusController, 1 endpoint) is the quick sold-out toggle on the Home page, which does the same marking through its own separate code. Both are live and both are used, so any change to how "sold out" behaves has to be made in both places.

functions.name: Publishing and history
functions.summary: Lets venue staff hold their menu edits as unpublished changes, see what is waiting, then send them all to the screens in one go — or throw them away. It also keeps a record of past publishes so a menu can be put back to how it looked before.

functions.name: Importing a menu from pasted text
functions.summary: Someone at a venue can paste the text of their menu and have the system turn it into a real menu: it reads the lines, spots which dishes it already knows about, and asks the person to settle anything it isn't sure of. They can then either create a brand-new menu from the result or overwrite an existing one, with a saved copy kept so the old menu can be put back.

functions.name: Registering and pairing screens
functions.summary: This is how a physical display gets turned into a screen the venue can send menus to. A device is either plugged in and shows a short code that someone types in to link it to the venue, or it is set up in advance before it ships so it connects itself the moment it is powered on.

lives.who: Screens themselves, plus platform staff for the final linking step

functions.builtTwice: Yes — the venue-side of this is built twice. Venue staff get it at /api/back-office/venues/{venueId}/screens (2 endpoints: add a screen, and register a screen in advance for a device being shipped out), and platform support staff get the same two things again at /api/platform-operations/venues/{venueId}/screens (2 endpoints), written separately. Both are live and both are called — venue staff use the first every day, support staff use the second when they set a venue up or step in to help. Changing how a screen is added, or how an advance registration works, means changing it in both places or the two drift apart.

functions.name: Managing screens
functions.summary: This is the day-to-day upkeep of the TV screens in a venue: seeing the list of screens and how each one is doing, naming them and setting where they hang and how they lay content out, pushing fresh content to one screen or all of them at once, and dealing with the physical boxes — restarting a screen that has gone odd, disconnecting a device, swapping a broken one for a new one that inherits everything, and shelving a screen the venue no longer uses.
functions.builtTwice: Yes — screen management is built twice, and both builds are live and in use. The venue-staff build (BackOfficeScreensController plus BackOfficePairingController) has 9 endpoints: list screens, edit a screen's name and display settings, push to one screen, push to all screens, restart a screen, archive or un-archive a screen, disconnect a device, and the two-step device replacement (preview then swap). The platform-support build (PlatformOperationsScreensController) has 4 endpoints, a narrower set covering the parts support staff need on a customer's behalf: list screens, edit a screen, push to one screen, push to all. The overlapping four exist in both places, so any change to how listing, editing, or pushing works has to be made in both builds or the two sides drift apart. The five that only venue staff have — restart, archive, disconnect, and the replacement pair — are things support staff cannot currently do through their own routes.

functions.name: Deciding what shows on which screen
functions.summary: This is how a venue decides what each screen in the room actually shows: putting a particular menu page onto a particular screen, taking it back off, seeing at a glance what every screen is currently showing and who put it there, and building a rotation of slides that a screen cycles through with its own timings and day/time windows. It also includes a preview that shows how many menu items will fit on a screen of a given size and which ones would spill off the bottom.
functions.builtTwice: Two parts of this function are built twice, in separate code. The slide rotation is built twice: once for venue staff (BackOfficePlaylistsController, 5 endpoints) and once for platform support staff (PlatformOperationsPlaylistsController, 5 endpoints). The "what fits on a screen" preview is also built twice: once for venue staff (BackOfficeScreensController, 1 endpoint) and once for platform support staff (PlatformOperationsScreensController, 1 endpoint). Both builds of each are live and in use, so any change to how rotations or the fit preview work has to be made in both places. The remaining part — assigning menu pages to screens and seeing what each screen is showing — is built once, for venue staff only (BackOfficeContentController, 6 endpoints); platform support staff have no equivalent.

functions.name: Video walls
functions.summary: Lets someone join two, three or four screens together into a named group that behaves as one big display, choose the arrangement (side by side, a row of three, or a two-by-two block) and say which screen sits in each position. The same group can later be broken up so every screen goes back to showing its own content.
functions.builtTwice: Yes — video walls are built twice, as two separate implementations. One serves venue staff working in the back office; the other serves platform support staff who need to set a wall up on a venue's behalf. Each build has the same three endpoints: list the walls, create or rearrange one, and break one up. Both are live and both are called, so any change to how video walls work has to be made in both places.

functions.name: Look and feel
functions.summary: Sets how a venue's screens look — background and accent colours, fonts, title and glow colours, and section colours — either by picking one of the ready-made designs (Bar Classic, Violet Lounge, Hot Summer, Ocean Dive, Rose Gold) or by choosing every colour and font by hand. It can also be reset back to the default look at any time.
functions.builtTwice: The main look-and-feel controls are built twice, as two separate sets of 6 endpoints. One set serves venue staff working in the back office; the other serves platform support staff acting on a venue's behalf. Both are live and both are used, so any change to how looks work — a new ready-made design, a new colour or font setting, a change to what resetting does — has to be made in both places or the two will drift apart. There is also a seventh, separate endpoint under the menu content area that lists the "menu looks" a venue could choose; it currently always comes back empty.

functions.name: Happy hour
functions.summary: Happy hour lets a venue set the times and days its happy hour runs, switch it on or off, and see whether it is running right now in the venue's own local time. There is also an override to force happy hour on or off no matter what the schedule says.
functions.builtTwice: Happy hour is built twice, as two separate pieces of code. One serves venue staff working in their own venue (2 endpoints: read the schedule, change it). The other serves platform support staff acting on any venue (2 endpoints: the same read and change). Both are live and both are called, so any change to how happy hour works — a new setting, a rule change, a fix — has to be made in both places.

functions.name: Meal periods
functions.summary: Meal periods let a venue set up its named parts of the day — breakfast, lunch, dinner and so on — each with its own start and end time, the days it runs, and optionally the layout, the menu it filters to, and the look it uses while it is on. The venue can add, edit, delete and reorder them, and the list warns about times that overlap and shows which period is running now and which comes next in the venue's own local time.
functions.builtTwice: Yes — meal periods are built twice, as two separate implementations. One serves venue staff working in their own venue (BackOfficeMealPeriodsController, 5 endpoints); the other serves platform support staff acting on any venue on a customer's behalf (PlatformOperationsMealPeriodsController, 5 endpoints). Both are live and both are called, so any change to how meal periods work — a new field, a rule change, a fix — has to be made in both places, and both have to keep working.

functions.name: Dated promotions
functions.summary: Lets someone set up a special message that runs on the venue's screens between a start date and an end date — a holiday special, for example — with its own wording and layout, and a priority that decides which one wins if several are running at once. Promotions can be edited or switched off at any time, and the screens pick up the change straight away; switching one off keeps the record rather than deleting it.
functions.builtTwice: This function is built twice — two separate builds, each with 4 endpoints. One serves venue staff working in their own venue's back office; the other serves platform support staff working on a venue on the customer's behalf. Both are live and both are called, so any change to how dated promotions work has to be made in both places.

functions.name: Urgent notices
functions.summary: Puts an urgent message — with an optional picture — straight onto one screen or every screen in a venue for a set number of minutes, so it takes over what people are watching. The message can be taken down early, and there is a running list of every urgent message ever sent, including the ones that have expired or been pulled.
functions.builtTwice: Yes — this function is built twice, as two separate pieces of code. One build serves venue staff working in their own venue (3 endpoints: see the history, send an urgent message, take one down early). The other serves platform support staff acting on a venue's behalf (the same 3 endpoints). Both are live, both are used, and both have to keep working — so any change to how urgent notices behave has to be made in both places.

functions.name: The tap list
functions.summary: The tap list is where a venue keeps the drinks currently on tap — grouped into categories like IPAs or Lagers, each drink with its style, strength, bitterness, price and colours, and marked available, sold out or coming soon. Categories and drinks can be added, edited, removed and dragged into the order they appear, and every change is pushed straight out to the venue's screens.
functions.builtTwice: The tap list is built twice, as two separate sets of code. One serves venue staff working on their own venue (9 endpoints, BackOfficeTapListController); the other serves platform support staff working on a venue on someone's behalf (9 endpoints, PlatformOperationsTapListController). Both are live and both are used, so any change to how the tap list works — a new field on a drink, a new rule about deleting a category — has to be made in both places, and tested in both, or the two sides drift apart.

functions.name: Till system connections
functions.builtTwice: Built three times, once per till brand, in three separate controllers: BackOfficeCloverPosController (5 endpoints), BackOfficeSquarePosController (5 endpoints) and BackOfficeToastPosController (3 endpoints). All three serve the same people — venue staff with permission to sync content — but each one talks to a different till company, so Clover and Square use a sign-in-and-approve flow with a return page, while Toast is linked by pasting in a restaurant ID and access token. All three are live and all three have to keep working, so a change to how till connections behave has to be made in each of the three.
functions.summary: Lets a venue link its till system — Clover, Square or Toast — to Vennusign, check whether that link is healthy and when it last synced, and pull the venue's items and categories across so they can be put on menus. The venue can also unlink the till at any time.

functions.name: What a screen on the wall calls
functions.summary: This is how a TV on the venue wall gets what it shows and stays in step: it asks for its current content — layout, colours, menu pages, any promotion, happy hour, playlist or emergency message — checks in to say it is alive, and confirms which version it actually put on the glass. It also holds an open live connection so a publish reaches it the moment it happens, and anyone standing at the venue can open a no-sign-in health page for a single screen.

functions.name: Incoming calls from Stripe and tills
functions.summary: This is how outside systems tell Vennusign that something has changed, without anyone logging in. Stripe reports subscription and payment changes so a venue's plan and hardware rental stay in step with billing, and a venue's till system (Square, Toast or Clover) reports menu or stock changes so the boards can be updated in the background.

functions.name: Managing venues across the platform
functions.summary: Lets Vennusign's own support staff look after every venue on the platform from one place: create a new venue, browse and filter the whole list, open a single venue to see its details, plan, screens and features, move it to a different plan, and hand-unlock or block an individual feature for it. They can also watch recent sign-ups and see how far each new customer got.

functions.name: Plans, feature switches and tiers
functions.summary: Platform staff set up the paid plans customers can be on — the price, the trial length, and the caps on how many screens and venues a plan allows — and decide which product features each plan includes. Turning a feature on or off for a plan immediately updates what every venue on that plan can do.

functions.name: Platform settings and moving them between environments
functions.summary: Platform staff can see and change the behind-the-scenes settings the software runs on — one environment at a time — with a full history of who changed what, the ability to put a setting back the way it was, and a safe way to copy a whole set of settings from one environment (say, the test one) into another (say, the live one), previewing every change before it happens. Secret values are never shown, and a change is refused if someone else has edited the same setting in the meantime.

functions.name: Test automation
functions.summary: Gives the automated test suite a few back-door controls over a test venue that no real person gets: wipe the venue clean before a run, lift its menu limit so a big run does not hit the ceiling, and backdate a stock change or a history entry so tests can check how the boards and history screens show older activity.

functions.name: Health and status

lives.who: Anyone, including monitoring tools and deployment scripts — no sign-in needed
lives.controller: Program (defined directly in the app's startup file, not a controller class)

functions.summary: Lets anyone confirm the service is up and see exactly which build and database version are running, and gives platform staff a single overview of the whole platform's health — how many venues and paying subscriptions there are, how many screens are online, offline or on an outdated app, and a running list of recent notable changes across all venues.

endpoints.p: Tells the signed-in back-office user who they are, which venue they are working in, which other venues they may switch to, and which features are switched on or off for them right now.
endpoints.who: back-office session (either an access-token venue login or a customer

endpoints.p: Shows the venue's billing page: its current plan and subscription status, how many screens and venues it is using against its limits, which other plans it could move to (and which features it would lose), plus any hardware-rental bundles and the venue's current hardware contract.
Checks that the venue is allowed to move to the plan it picked, then opens the Stripe billing portal so the owner can change their plan there.
Opens the Stripe billing portal so the venue owner can manage their payment details and subscription.
Starts a Stripe checkout so the venue owner can buy a software plan, billed monthly or yearly, after confirming the venue is eligible for that plan.
Starts a Stripe checkout so the venue owner can rent screen hardware on a fixed-term bundle.
Tells the menu screens which timezone the venue is in, what its size limits are, and how many menus it has.
Tells the menu builder its settings: the biggest import file allowed, how long to wait before warning about a stuck publish, and how much history to keep.
Lists every menu the venue has, with what its screens are currently showing, how many unpublished changes are waiting, and which screens it is on.
Tells the venue how many menus it is allowed and how many it is already using.
Shows the version of one menu that its screens are showing right now.
Makes a copy of a menu that shares the same dishes but is not yet published or on any screen.
Lists the pages of a menu in order.
Adds a new named page to a menu.
Renames a page of a menu.
Puts a menu's pages into a new order, refusing if someone else changed the pages in the meantime.
Makes a copy of one page inside the same menu.
Removes a page from a menu, either moving its sections to another page or deleting them, and reports how many screens lost their assignment.
Gives staff one screen showing every menu that is live on a screen, which dishes are sold out, and which screens are showing what, so they can quickly mark things unavailable.
Marks a dish as sold out (or back on) and it disappears from or reappears on every screen immediately, without a publish.
Puts every sold-out dish back on sale in one go, across all screens.
Lists which dishes are currently marked sold out, who changed them and when.
Shows what has changed in a menu since it was last sent to the screens.
Throws away all unpublished edits, putting the menu back to what the screens are showing.
Sends all of a menu's waiting changes to its screens, all at once or not at all.
Puts a menu away (archives it) or brings it back onto the shelf; a menu still on screens must be taken off first.
Shows the record of publishes and other events for a menu, limited to the venue's retention depth.
Shows the history of one page of a menu.
Restores a menu to an earlier published version as a set of unpublished changes that still need a publish to reach the screens.
Lists which menu page each screen has been assigned, and who assigned it.
Lists every screen in the venue with what it is showing, its online status, size and the publish that put it there.
Puts a menu page on a screen, either replacing what is there or adding it to the screen's rotation.
Takes one menu page off one screen.
Saves a whole set of screen changes for a menu at once — which pages go on which screens, replacing, rotating or removing.
Queues taking a menu off all its screens; it happens on the next publish rather than immediately.
Opens a menu in the builder: the working version, what has changed, and when it was last published.
Adds a new section (like 'Starters') to a menu page.
Renames a section of a menu.
Removes a section after the user chooses whether its dishes move to another section or go back to the library.
Moves a whole section, with its dishes, to a different page of the same menu.
Puts a menu's sections into a new order, refusing if someone else changed them in the meantime.
Puts the dishes in a section into a new order, refusing if the section changed in the meantime.
Drags a dish from one section to another on the same page, sending both sections' orders so nothing moves if the page changed.
Adds a dish to a section, either one already in the venue's library or a brand-new one typed in with an optional price; if it is already on the menu it says where.
Takes a dish off a menu page while keeping it in the venue's library for later.
Moves a dish into a section on a page (used by undo/redo), checking the section still looks the way it did before applying.
Edits a dish's name, description, price or listed status; name and description change everywhere, price changes only for this placement unless 'everywhere' is chosen.
Searches the venue's whole dish library by name, saying which menus each dish is already on.
Lists the menu looks (themes) the venue could choose; currently always empty.

Shows a venue user everything in their menu editor at once: all menus, their sections, the items in each section, and which extra features (happy hour, allergen badges, quick update) the venue can use.
Lets a venue user add a new, empty menu by giving it a name.
Lets a venue user rename one of their menus.
Lets a venue user mark a menu item as sold out or back in stock from the Home page, and pushes that change to the screens showing it right away.
Lets a venue user paste the text of a menu to begin an import; the system reads the lines, matches them against items the venue already has, and comes back with the questions it needs answered.
Shows a venue user the imports they started but have not finished, so they can pick one up again from the Menus home page.
Lets a venue user throw away an unfinished import instead of waiting for it to expire.
Shows a venue user the current state of one import: the parsed lines, the review questions, and the answers given so far.
Lets a venue user answer one review question about a pasted line, for example choosing whether it is a new item or the same as an item the venue already has.
Lets a venue user accept in one click every line the system is confident is the same as an existing item, instead of answering those questions one by one.
Lets a venue user tell the import that a pasted line is a section heading (like 'Desserts') rather than a dish, and re-reads the paste with that correction.
Lets a venue user undo marking a pasted line as a section heading, so it goes back to being treated as a dish.
Lets a venue user say the import should become a brand-new menu, and what to call it.
Lets a venue user finish the import by actually creating the new menu with the reviewed items.
Lets a venue user choose an existing menu that the import will overwrite, and shows a preview of what would change.
Lets a venue user finish the import by replacing the chosen existing menu's contents with the reviewed items, keeping a saved copy of the old version.
Lets a venue user put a menu back the way it was before an import replaced it, using the saved copy.
Registers a screen in advance for a device that will be shipped to the venue, handing back a one-time setup token the device uses to connect itself when it arrives.
Shows the venue's list of screens with each one's status, settings, and latest content-delivery information.
Adds a new screen to the venue with default display settings, ready to be paired with a device later.
Lets venue staff rename a screen and change its location and display settings such as layout, photo grid density, split ratio, and how long the hero image stays up.
Immediately sends the venue's current content to one screen instead of waiting for its normal refresh.
Archives a screen the venue no longer uses, or brings an archived screen back into service.
Forces a misbehaving screen to start over by marking it offline so it reconnects and fetches everything fresh.
Disconnects a physical device from the venue's screen so the device no longer shows this venue's content and can be paired elsewhere.
Sends the latest content to every active screen in the venue at once and reports how many screens were reached.
Previews which menu items will fit on a screen that shows a set number of items, and which ones will spill off the bottom.
Lists the venue's video walls - named groups of screens that act together as one big display - and which screen sits in each position.
Creates or rearranges a video wall by naming it, picking a layout of 2, 3, or 4 screens, and assigning which screen goes where.
Breaks up a video wall so each of its screens goes back to showing content on its own.
Links a new device to the signed-in venue by entering the pairing code the device is showing on its screen.

endpoints.p: Checks whether a new device can take over an existing screen's job and shows what would carry over - name, settings, history, and video-wall spot - before anything changes.
endpoints.who: Back-office session (venue from session claim), screen.device.pair (cl

endpoints.p: Swaps a broken screen's device for a new one so the screen keeps its name, settings, history, and place in any video wall.
endpoints.who: Back-office session (venue from session claim), screen.device.pair (cl

endpoints.p: Shows the ordered list of slides a screen rotates through.
Adds a new slide to a screen's rotation, with its content, how long it stays up, and an optional daily time window and days of the week.
Edits an existing slide - its content, timing, schedule, or whether it is switched on.
Rearranges the order the slides play in.
Removes a slide from the screen's rotation.
Lists the ready-made theme designs a venue can pick from.
Shows the venue's current look - its colors and fonts as displayed on screens.
Changes the venue's basic look: background color, accent color, and font.
Gives finer control over the board's appearance: title and glow colors, board background, up to four section colors, glow strength, and separate title and item fonts.
Applies one of the ready-made designs to the venue in a single step.
Throws away the venue's customizations and puts the screens back on the default look.
Shows a venue owner every date-based promotion they have set up for their venue, including ones that have been switched off.
Lets a venue owner add a new promotion that runs between two dates (e.g. a holiday special) with an optional title, message and screen layout, then tells the venue's screens something changed.
Lets a venue owner change an existing date-based promotion's dates, wording, priority or on/off state, and notifies the venue's screens.
Lets a venue owner switch off a promotion so it stops appearing on screens; the record is kept rather than removed.
Shows a venue owner all emergency messages ever sent to their screens, including expired and cancelled ones.
Lets a venue owner push an urgent message (with optional picture link) onto one screen or every screen in the venue for a set number of minutes, and pushes it to those screens immediately.
Lets a venue owner take an emergency message down from screens before its time is up.
Shows a venue owner their happy hour schedule and whether happy hour is running right now in the venue's local time.
Lets a venue owner set the daily happy hour start and end time, which days it runs, whether it is on, and whether to force it on or off regardless of the clock.
Shows a venue owner their meal periods (breakfast, lunch, dinner and so on), flags any that overlap, and says which one is on now and which comes next in venue local time.

Finishes adding a new passkey by checking the browser's answer and saving the passkey to the account.
Starts a passkey sign-in for the given email address by giving the browser the challenge to sign.
Finishes a passkey sign-in, logs the customer in with a strong (MFA-satisfied) session, and sets the session cookie.

Finishes authenticator-app setup by checking the first code and handing the customer their one-time recovery codes.
Upgrades the customer's current session to strong (MFA-satisfied) by checking a code from their authenticator app.
Upgrades the customer's current session to strong by spending one of their one-time recovery codes.

Lets a new customer create their first venue (name, timezone, type, languages) once they have a plan.

Creates a new venue record (name, timezone, type, languages) and returns its id.

endpoints.p: Lets a Vennusign support person look at all of a venue's menus, sections and item groups without being able to change anything.
Shows a support person the venue's meal periods (breakfast, lunch, dinner, etc.), any overlapping ones, which is active right now and which comes next.
Lets a support person add a new meal period to a venue with its times, days, layout, menu filter and theme.
Lets a support person change an existing meal period's name, times, days, layout, menu filter or theme.
Lets a support person remove a meal period from a venue.
Lets a support person change the order the venue's meal periods are listed in.
Shows a support person the venue's happy hour schedule and whether happy hour is on right now.
Lets a support person set the venue's happy hour times and days, turn it on or off, or force it on or off regardless of the schedule.
Shows a support person the venue's date-based promotions (e.g. a holiday special running between two dates).
Lets a support person add a promotion that shows on the venue's screens between a start and end date, and pushes the change to screens immediately.
Lets a support person edit an existing promotion's dates, wording, priority or on/off state, and pushes the change to screens.
Lets a support person retire a promotion so it no longer shows, and pushes the change to screens.

Lets a support person put an urgent message (optionally with an image) on all of a venue's screens, or on one chosen screen, for a set number of minutes, and pushes it out immediately.
Lets a support person take an emergency message off the screens early.
Shows a support person the venue's beer tap list: the categories and all the beers in them.
Lets a support person add a tap list category (e.g. IPAs) with an optional shared price, and pushes it to screens.
Lets a support person rename a tap list category, change its price or switch it on or off, and pushes it to screens.
Lets a support person remove a tap list category, as long as no beers are still filed under it.
Lets a support person add a beer to the tap list with its style, strength, price, colours and availability, and pushes it to screens.
Lets a support person edit a beer on the tap list (details, price, sold out, coming soon), and pushes it to screens.
Lets a support person remove a beer from the tap list and pushes the change to screens.
Lets a support person change the order tap list categories appear on screen.
Lets a support person change the order beers appear on screen.

Lets a support person add a slide to a screen's rotation.
Lets a support person edit one slide in a screen's rotation.
Lets a support person change the order slides play in on a screen.
Lets a support person remove a slide from a screen's rotation.
Lets platform staff set up a screen for a venue ahead of time and get a one-off setup code so the physical device can claim it when it is plugged in.
Lists all the screens that belong to a venue, with their name, location, status and display settings.
Adds a new, not-yet-paired screen to a venue with a name and optional location.
Renames a screen or changes where it is and how it lays out content (photo grid density, layout, split ratio, how long a hero image stays up).
Forces one screen to refresh and pick up the latest content right now.
Forces every active screen in a venue to refresh and pick up the latest content, and reports how many screens were told to.
Shows which menu items would fit on a screen that holds a set number of items (4, 6, 8 or 9) and which would be cut off, using the venue's oldest active menu.
Lists the groups of screens that have been joined together to act as one big video wall.
Creates or replaces a named video wall by joining 2, 3 or 4 screens together in a 2x1, 3x1 or 2x2 arrangement.
Breaks up a named video wall so its screens go back to working on their own.
Lists the built-in ready-made looks (Bar Classic, Violet Lounge, Hot Summer, Ocean Dive, Rose Gold) a venue can pick for its screens.
Shows the colours and fonts a venue's screens currently use.
Sets a venue's basic look: background colour, accent colour and font (Inter, Georgia or Arial).
Sets a venue's detailed custom look: title colour, glow colour and strength, board background, section colours, and title/item fonts.
Applies one of the ready-made looks to a venue's screens by its key.
Wipes a venue's custom look and puts its screens back to the default colours and fonts.
Tells platform staff whether the database-backed settings loader is switched on, when it last loaded successfully, and whether its last attempt failed.

endpoints.p: Changes one system setting's value for an environment, refusing if someone else changed it since it was loaded.

endpoints.p: Removes the stored value for one system setting in an environment so it falls back to its default.
endpoints.who: platform-ops API key with Configuration:edit permission; secret settin

endpoints.p: Shows the change history of one system setting in an environment so staff can see what it used to be and who changed it.
endpoints.who: platform-ops API key with Configuration:read permission

endpoints.p: Puts a system setting back to an earlier version from its history, refusing if the setting changed in the meantime.
endpoints.who: platform-ops API key with Configuration:admin permission

endpoints.p: Downloads a bundle of an environment's non-secret system settings so they can be copied to another environment.
endpoints.who: platform-ops API key with Configuration:import permission

endpoints.p: Shows what would change if a settings bundle were applied to a target environment, item by item, without changing anything.
endpoints.who: platform-ops API key with Configuration:import permission

endpoints.p: Applies a previously previewed settings bundle to a target environment, refusing if any setting changed since the preview.
endpoints.who: platform-ops API key with Configuration:import permission
